newsitem.title: USA: ASARCO opts for synthetic puts to cover price risk.
newsitem.headline: ASARCO opts for synthetic puts to cover price risk.

text.p: ASARCO Inc said it will use synthetic put options to cover downside price risk on some of its 1997 production, replacing regular puts which have become too expensive following the Sumitomo scandal.
"I am not aware of anybody else doing this," ASARCO's chairman, president and chief executive, Richard de J Osborne, told reporters following an analyst briefing last week.
So-called synthetic puts refer to the twin act of buying call options and selling production forward to obtain a price protection similar to the single act of buying put options.

Banks and others who sold over-the-counter puts last year as cheap floor price insurance for producers got their fingers burned when the unexpected crash in copper prices following Sumitomo's huge losses forced them to pay out as puts come into the money.
With no more cheap insurance around, U.S. producers have either opted to have no protection or find other forms of risk coverage.

ASARCO has bought calls at a strike price of $1.04 on 149.5 million pounds of production "spread evenly throughout the year". The second leg will be to sell forward 149.5 million pounds of production at $1.04 or above, Osborne said.
If copper is sold forward above the strike price, the calls will effectively be free. ASARCO produced more than a billion pounds of copper last year.
"If the copper price keeps going up, then we may decide to keep the calls open and keep us long in copper," Osborne said.
Contrary to most industry analysts, ASARCO is forecasting a modest copper supply deficit this year, and a larger deficit in 1998.
"The forward price of copper is not over $1.04 at the present time so we are not covered," Osborne said.

A derivatives specialist at an LME ring dealing member said precious metals producers have been using synthetic puts for many years, and it was "unusual but not irregular" for a base metals producer to use them.

"But it's very unusual to buy the calls first. People usually sell forward first," the specialist said. "And if you did both at the same time you save yourself some money because you don't pay a spread."
"As long as they are doing some hedging for 1998, it seems fair that ASARCO can take a chance for 1997 because prices are not going to collapse this year," the specialist added.
ASARCO's cash costs are in th "mid 60 cents per pound", Osborne said. The bulk of the company's output is from the traditionally higher cost sulphide production.
On an annual basis, ASARCO's earnings have become slightly more sensitive to changes in copper prices as the New York based company cranks up output to more than a billion pounds a year.
For each cent change in copper prices, ASARCO's shares are impacted by 16 cents on an annual basis, based on this year's output. This is up from 15.4 cents per share last year.
